items.note: Product design course comparing an AI-integrated instruction group with a conventionally taught group on creativity gains; abstract not reachable (OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC, Springer page all failed), so classified from search notes, which say measures may be partly survey-based and N and allocation are unstated.

Study of generative-AI availability on university students' emotions and creative problem-solving performance (a linked data record calls it a quasi-experiment in design education); abstract not reachable (OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC, ScienceDirect 403), so classified from title and notes; do not confuse with the PsyArXiv ChatGPT creative problem-solving experiment (10.31234/osf.io/9z2tc), which has a different author.

Randomized controlled experiment with third-year engineering students comparing ChatGPT-assisted and unassisted ideation (728 ideas) plus a survey; no significant difference in ideation outcomes between groups; abstract gives the number of ideas but not of students; distinct from the same first author's 2026 crossover study.

Two controlled ChatGPT experiments (N = 234, 205), a Gemini replication (N = 157), and 6,290 naturalistic chats relate measured Creative Direction to originality and to semantic similarity across users; direction is measured, not assigned, and the abstract does not state an AI versus no-AI arm (it mentions creativity measured without LLM assistance, so check for a within-person comparison); may end up context_observational.

Eight-week control-group design with 36 preservice Turkish teachers writing STEM stories with AI tools (19) or without (17); stories scored on textuality criteria, main outcomes are digital literacy and 21st-century skills scales; abstract says the groups were 'randomly selected', possibly intact groups rather than individuals; below the 50-participant threshold.

Process study coding 591 turns from 14 students (dyads) ideating with ChatGPT examples; all participants use ChatGPT, there is no comparison condition and no creativity score, only cognitive-strategy categories (most ideas repeated ChatGPT's).

Exploratory study in one high-school class where students wrote short stories alone or with ChatGPT 3.5, with ChatGPT-only stories added; stories compared quantitatively and qualitatively and judged by a same-age reading group; class size not stated, likely well under 50.

Sixty reading-club members divided evenly to write horror stories alone or with Claude AI on identical prompts; stories rated on originality, coherence, horror effect, character development, and impact; unassisted writers did slightly better; assignment method not stated.

One-factor between-subjects lab brainstorming experiment comparing nominal, interactive, hybrid human-plus-GPT-3, and AI-only groups on idea count and creativity; conference abstract (AOM Proceedings) does not state N (search notes say 168) or random assignment.

Public gamified deployment (832 participants, 15,719 generated images) with a 2x2 design varying the AI target agent's emotional expressiveness and a novelty reward; all participants use the same image generator, so the AI manipulation concerns the AI audience, not assistance; kept as experiment on the doubt rule, but likely out at full text (expressiveness left creative output unchanged; novelty reward sustained diversity).
